extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional/political theory; statesmen and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance on how statesmen, Parliament (Commons and Lords), and the Crown should behave within the English constitutional system; focuses on communication, prudence in exercising power, and institutional interaction. Drawn from a didactic introduction to a book on the English Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmen should lead the public, not follow
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal statesmen ought to lead the public, and not let the public lead them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in 'quiet times' when statesmen have discretion they must settle which questions to deal with. In times of public perturbation the public tendency strongly determines topics, but in quiet times statesmen have great power and responsibility to choose and shape public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantic and doctrinaire tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman should not assume a pedantic/doctrinaire tone or proclaim superiority to his audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English people detest a tone that implies 'I am better than you; I have studied this as you have not.' Such gaucherie shows defect of imagination and incapacity for dealing with men; it is an anti-pattern for a guide or instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give clear, manly conclusions rather than long argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Much argument is not required to guide the public; what is mostly needed is the manly utterance of clear conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A felicitous expression of clear conclusions (with a few light humorous illustrations if appropriate) suffices: 'He will have given the text, the scribes in the newspapers will write the sermon.' Over-elaboration is unnecessary for public guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmen should show their own nature and speak palpably
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman ought to show his own nature and talk in a palpable way about what is to him important truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal authenticity and straightforward expression help both to guide and to benefit the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept or reiterate the decisions of ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman must not accept or reiterate decisions born of popular ignorance merely to curry favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a statesman reiterates ignorant decisions he becomes 'the hireling of the nation' and harms it. This is contrasted with leading and educating the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties should not bid for the working-man's support by promising to do as he likes
rubrics_metrics.description: Political parties must not corrupt themselves by simply promising to do whatever working-class voters demand in order to secure their votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such competition to defer to the uneducated decision-maker ('Vox populi will be Vox diaboli') is deeply corrupting and dangerous for both the voters and the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid policies that permanently unite lower classes as a class
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmen should avoid raising questions or measures that will permanently combine the working-classes as a political class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a particular measure will have that effect depends on particulars, but permanent organized supremacy of the lower orders (in their present state) is an evil because it substitutes numbers/ignorance for knowledge/instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher orders must remove actual and seeming grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Those in higher orders must avoid every evil and every appearance of evil; remove not only every actual grievance but where possible every seeming grievance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should willingly concede every claim which can be safely conceded to prevent having to concede more harmful claims under pressure later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fighting losing battles that strengthen the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage in long, well-fought losing battles which may teach the lower orders to combine and thereby strengthen the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combative propensities lead men to prefer fighting even losing battles; statesmanship requires seeing that a battle may strengthen the enemy and thus be a strategic mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Lords must yield when Commons' opinion equals the nation's decided will
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords should yield whenever the opinion of the Commons is also the opinion of the nation and it is clear the nation has made up its mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the nation has decided is to be judged by all the circumstances (majorities, diversity of organs conveying opinion, unanimity, etc.). This is a practical judgement, not a mechanical formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical/formal tests for national determination
rubrics_metrics.description: It is dangerous to adopt a fixed mechanical test (e.g., counting how many times a Bill is sent up) for deciding whether the nation is determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such rules could permit the Lords to ignore facts of real life and decide by abstract formula (and could have allowed rejection of the Reform Act 1832). Number of retries is an indication but only one of several.

rubrics_metrics.name: On first-class subjects the Lords should be very slow to reject Bills passed by large Commons majorities
rubrics_metrics.description: As an approximate practical rule, on important subjects the Lords ought to be very slow to reject a Bill passed even once by a large majority of the Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not an unvarying rule: majorities may be genuine or fictitious; the real test is whether the majorities embody representative opinion as well as constituency opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid division between Lords and Commons which weakens resistance to uneducated majority
rubrics_metrics.description: A dissension between Lords and Commons divides the resisting power of educated classes and is politically harmful when facing uneducated majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lords and Commons share the interest of preventing rule by uneducated members; they should avoid bidding against each other for the aid of the common opponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy should cultivate and use the homage of new wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The aristocracy should accept and skilfully use the worship/homage of newly-made wealth to preserve their headship of the plutocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repelling such homage is folly; political utility arises from ancient wealth being revered by new wealth, which can be politically harnessed to preserve influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the House of Lords' social influence beyond mere electioneering
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords exerts an incalculably greater influence over society while it exists than it would if abolished; its influence acts more on individuals (social prestige) than as an overt electioneering force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social influence often operates privately (families, female influence) and can be politically useful if managed properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: If the House of Lords is to retain influence, exercise power timidly and cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: The great power of the House of Lords should be exercised timidly and cautiously; yield many points rather than risk the foundation of their power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yielding minor points and giving large donations out of income (to preserve capital) keeps their 'capital' of influence intact; historical example: Duke of Wellington's guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life peerages are not a benign fix unless used extensively — they carry risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Life peerages cannot remedy the contrast between Houses unless very numerous; creating many life peers without major upheaval is unlikely and may presage or accompany revolution destroying hereditary principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moderate number of life peers will usually counsel moderation and be politically useful, but relying on life peerages as a structural fix is dangerous unless one accepts wider constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment is an ancient check against gross misuse of prerogative but limited for minor mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The impeachment process can check gross excesses (e.g., advising the Queen into measures endangering the realm), but it is not a remedy for bona fide errors of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misuses that are errors of judgment (not intended to harm) cannot appropriately be punished by treason law; the practical remedy for such misuses is political: a change of Ministry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of Ministry is the general remedy for misuse of prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: Where prerogative is misused in good faith or via errors of judgment, the main practical remedy is to replace the Ministry rather than legal punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This political sanction usually works well because ministers weigh the risk of dismissal; however, it has limits (only Commons can decisively remove Ministers by vote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties/foreign engagements should not be left to a secret committee alone — submit them to Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper that treaties and important foreign agreements should be committed to the discretion of a single secret committee without consulting Parliament or the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties are as important as laws and deserve representative assent; no other select committee has comparable power, and allowing such discretion is anomalous even if sometimes beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional homogeneity between Chambers is undesirable; deliberation by Parliament improves foreign policy decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the two Chambers were homogeneously and harmoniously identical, that would be a defect; submitting foreign arrangements to Parliament is preferable when both Houses are reasonable and predisposed to think the Government right but able to confront facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity between Houses provides checks and deliberation that benefit important decisions, especially foreign policy.
